title: Write Epilogue — The Accord
steps: Write the epilogue for "The Accord". Genre slug: political-scifi.

response.assistant_message: Queuing the epilogue for 'The Accord' — I'll let you know when it's ready.

result.content_text:
The tram from Cornavin arrived four minutes early, which Mara took as a bad sign. Good luck never announced itself.

She stood on the pavement outside the Palais des Nations and let the other passengers flow around her, a cluster of junior delegates in lanyards, a camera crew wrestling a tripod case through the turnstile gate, two men in identical grey suits who moved with the particular unhurried certainty of people who carried weapons under their jackets. She watched the two men until they cleared the security arch, then looked away.

The morning was cold and very bright. Geneva in November wore its light like a warning: thin, flat, offering no warmth. The Palais stretched along the ridge above the lake, its stone facade the colour of old teeth, its rows of tall windows reflecting nothing but cloud. Flags of a hundred and ninety-three member states hung from their poles in the windless air, perfectly still, as if they too were waiting to see how this went.

Mara checked her watch. Forty minutes before the session opened.

She put her hand against her ribs, pressing through the wool of her jacket until she felt the slight, hard outline of the drive, no larger than a thumbnail, stitched into the lining last night with a needle and thread borrowed from the hotel sewing kit, her fingers clumsy and slow at midnight while Yusuf's voice came through her earpiece from Nairobi, talking her through the file structure one more time.

*The weighting tables are on the second partition,* he had said. *If she opens those and understands what she's reading, that's enough. You don't need her to believe you. You need her to doubt.*

She needed Hartmann. That was the whole of it.

Vance would have a security detail inside, not uniformed, nothing so obvious, but people placed at the access points to the delegations' corridor, people whose job this morning was to ensure that nothing reached the German ambassador before she cast her vote. Mara had spent the train journey from Stuttgart calculating the gaps in that coverage, turning the problem the way she turned an endgame position: not looking for a winning move, not yet, but identifying which squares were controlled and which were not.

She had one credential that still worked. Her UN Office of Treaty Compliance badge, which Vance's team had suspended at eleven o'clock last night, she had received the automated email at eleven forty-three, lying on the hotel bed in her clothes, and had understood at once that the suspension itself told her something useful. They had moved when they moved, not sooner. That meant they were not certain what she had. If they had known about the drive, about Yusuf's data, the suspension would have come days ago.

What she also had, tucked in the breast pocket of her jacket, was a temporary observer credential issued three weeks earlier for the pre-ratification technical review, a paper credential, pale blue, laminated, with her photograph and a barcode that had not yet been deactivated because nobody in the building's access-control office worked before eight-thirty, and it was currently seven fifty-four.

She had twenty-two minutes in which that credential still functioned, assuming no one had thought to flag it manually.

She walked toward the gate.

The security arch beeped for the woman ahead of her, a delegate who had forgotten a phone in her coat pocket, and the guard waved her through the manual lane with the bored efficiency of someone who had done this a thousand times. Mara kept her pace steady. She set her bag on the conveyor, held the blue credential against the reader, and looked at the guard's face rather than the screen.

He glanced at the credential. Glanced at her face. Looked at the screen.

The light went green.

She picked up her bag on the other side and did not hurry., -

The delegations' corridor on the second floor smelled of floor wax and old radiator heat, a smell Mara associated with every formal building she had ever worked in, as if institutions produced the same olfactory signature regardless of country. She had been in this corridor forty or fifty times. She knew which way the German delegation's suite faced, knew the small anteroom where the ambassador's personal staff set up before sessions, knew that Hartmann arrived between thirty and twenty minutes before any vote, never later, because Hartmann's punctuality was the kind that made other people feel ashamed of their own.

She also knew that the two men in grey suits had come up in the lift ahead of her.

She could see one of them now, stationed near the junction where the corridor branched toward the main chamber. He was reading something on his phone with the focused non-attention of a man whose real attention was on the corridor. His colleague would be at the other end, near the emergency stairwell. Between them they controlled the approach to the German suite.

Mara stopped at the water fountain and drank, slowly, watching him over the curve of the chrome fixture.

He had not looked at her yet. That would change the moment she moved toward the German suite.

She straightened up, turned, and walked in the opposite direction, toward the small conference room that the Swiss delegation used for pre-session briefings, which shared a connecting door with the anteroom of the German suite. The connecting door was usually locked. She had seen it propped open twice in three years, both times when the Swiss and German delegations were coordinating on the same agenda item.

Today's agenda item was the Accord.

She tried the handle.

The door opened.

The anteroom was empty, no staff yet, no Hartmann, but the main suite door was ajar, and through it came the sound of a chair being moved, a briefcase set down on a table, the small sounds of someone arranging their morning. Mara stepped through the connecting door and pulled it closed behind her.

"Ms. Voss."

Hartmann was standing at the window, still in her coat, looking out at the lake. She had not turned around. She was a compact woman with close-cropped silver hair and the particular stillness of someone who had learned, over decades, to take up exactly as much space as she needed and no more. On the table behind her, beside a stack of briefing folders, was a silver-framed photograph, a man in his sixties, laughing at something off-camera, squinting in bright summer light.

"Ambassador." Mara kept her voice level. "I need four minutes."

"You shouldn't be in this building." Hartmann turned from the window. Her face was not hostile, which was almost worse. It was careful. "Your credentials were suspended."

"I have something you need to see before you vote."

"Mara." Hartmann said her name the way people said it when they were about to explain something painful. "I know what you believe about the algorithm. I've read Vance's rebuttal. The technical review, "

"Was conducted by the team that designed the flaw." Mara reached into her jacket, felt for the seam, pressed her thumbnail into the thread until it gave. The drive came loose into her palm. "This is six years of resource-allocation mortality data from sub-Saharan Africa, compiled by an epidemiologist named Yusuf Adeyemi. He's been trying to get a meeting with the treaty office for eight months. No one would see him." She set the drive on the table, next to the photograph of Hartmann's husband. "The weighting tables in SOVEREIGN's founding algorithm will systematically deprioritise the Global South during resource scarcity events. Not as an oversight. As a design feature."

Hartmann looked at the drive. She did not pick it up.

"The session opens in thirty-one minutes," she said.

"I know."

"If I delay my vote, the German bloc delays. The ratification timetable collapses. We lose the window." She looked up. "Do you understand what losing the window means? The 2038 thermal event killed my husband. Eleven thousand people in three weeks. The Accord is the only binding framework that, "

"It will kill more than eleven thousand." Mara heard her own voice come out quieter than she intended, which was perhaps the right register. "Not in three weeks. Over thirty years. Quietly. In places where the data doesn't make the front page." She touched the edge of the drive with one finger. "Four minutes. That's all I'm asking. Open the second partition. Look at the weighting tables. You'll see it."

The door to the corridor opened.

One of the grey-suited men filled the frame. Behind him, Mara could hear the second set of footsteps approaching.

Hartmann looked at the man in the doorway. Then she looked at Mara. Then she looked at the drive on the table beside her husband's photograph.

The man in the doorway said, "Ambassador, this individual does not have valid access to, "

"Thank you," Hartmann said, in a tone that closed the sentence like a door. "Wait outside."

A pause. The man in the doorway did not move.

"Outside," Hartmann said again.

He withdrew. The door did not quite close.

Hartmann picked up the drive. She turned it once in her fingers, a small, almost weightless thing, the kind of object that should not matter and did, and then she crossed to the desk in the corner where her laptop sat open, its screen still showing the session agenda.

Mara watched her plug it in and felt something shift in her chest: not relief, not yet, not anything so clean. The fear that had been with her since Stuttgart, since the hotel room, since the moment she had first read Yusuf's summary and understood what she was looking at, that fear did not leave. It simply changed shape.

Because Hartmann was reading now, and the man in the grey suit was standing six feet away on the other side of a door that had not latched, and in twenty-nine minutes the session would open with or without the German ambassador's vote, and Mara had no idea what Hartmann would do when she reached the weighting tables and saw what was there.

She only knew that somewhere in this building, Elias Vance was already being told.

The silence in the room had a particular quality, the held-breath silence of someone reading something they cannot unread.

Hartmann's eyes moved across the screen in the focused, line-by-line way of a person who had spent thirty years parsing treaty language and knew exactly where the weight of a document lived. Her coat was still on. She had not sat down. One hand rested flat on the desk beside the laptop, the fingers slightly spread, as though she needed the contact with something solid.

Mara stood three feet back and watched her and did not speak.

The weighting tables were on the second partition, clearly labelled, the column headers in the clean sans-serif font that SOVEREIGN's interface team had chosen because it looked neutral. *Resource Priority Index. Allocation Coefficient. Scarcity Threshold Modifier.* The numbers beneath those headers were not neutral. They had never been neutral. That was the point.

Hartmann reached the tables. Mara knew the moment it happened because the older woman's hand, the one flat on the desk, curled slowly into a fist.

"These coefficients," Hartmann said. Her voice had changed, not louder, not broken, something more careful than either. "The scarcity threshold modifier for sub-Saharan Africa is point three one."

"Yes."

"Western Europe is point eight seven."

"Yes."

Hartmann straightened. She did not look at Mara yet. "That means in a resource scarcity event, SOVEREIGN will begin rationing allocations to sub-Saharan Africa at a third of the threshold it applies to Western Europe."

"At point three one of the threshold. So by the time the system begins protecting European populations, African populations will have been in engineered scarcity for, depending on the severity of the event, between eight and fourteen months."

Hartmann turned. Her face was not what Mara had expected. She had braced for anger, for the defensive rigidity of someone whose life's work was being called into question. What she saw instead was something quieter and more frightening: a woman doing arithmetic in her head, and not liking the answer.

"Vance told me the regional coefficients reflected existing infrastructure capacity," Hartmann said. "That the system was calibrated to work with what each region already had. He called it a *realistic baseline.*"

"It is a realistic baseline. It's realistic in the way that locking someone in a burning building and saying *the exits reflect existing structural capacity* is realistic." Mara stopped herself. This was not the moment for that kind of language. "The coefficients don't adjust upward as infrastructure improves. They're fixed in the founding algorithm. Locked at ratification. The only mechanism for revision requires a unanimous Security Council vote."

Hartmann's eyes went back to the screen. "Which will never happen."

"Which has never happened. In the history of the Security Council."

A long silence. Through the unlatched door, Mara could hear the man in the grey suit shifting his weight.

"There's something else," Mara said.

She had not planned to say it this way. She had planned to lead with the data, let the weighting tables do the work, and only then, if there was time, if Hartmann was still listening, bring out the second thing. But Hartmann was listening, and there was no way to make sense of Vance's choices, the depth of them, the architecture of deliberate blindness he had constructed, without the second thing.

She reached into her bag and took out three printed pages. She had printed them in the hotel business centre at six that morning, on paper she had fed into the machine herself, and she had folded them twice and put them in the outer pocket where she could reach them without looking.

She set them on the desk beside the laptop.

"In November 2019," she said, "a Norwegian signals intelligence station in Reykjavik intercepted a transmission. Non-terrestrial origin. The signal was analysed over fourteen months by a classified joint team. The conclusion of that analysis, which was buried at the highest classification level and shared with fewer than twenty people, was that the transmission was structured. Intentional. And that it was moving toward us."

Hartmann looked at the pages. She did not touch them.

"The team's assessment," Mara continued, "was that humanity had a window, their estimate was thirty years, give or take, to present a unified, resource-stable civilisation. Or be assessed as unfit." She kept her voice flat, factual, the way she would present a treaty compliance finding. The flatness was the only way she could say it at all. "Elias Vance was the civilian liaison who received the initial report. He has had access to the full file since January 2020."

The room was very still.

Hartmann picked up the pages. She read the first one, the summary sheet, the one with the signal coordinates and the classification header and the date, and Mara watched the colour leave her face the way colour left a room when a cloud crossed the sun. Not dramatic. Just gone.

"He knew this," Hartmann said. It was not a question.

"When he came to you. When he showed you the Accord framework. When he told you that the ratification window was critical, that missing it would be catastrophic, that the timeline was non-negotiable." Mara kept her eyes on Hartmann's face. "He knew this."

Hartmann set the pages down. She turned to look at the silver-framed photograph on the table, the man laughing in summer light, the squint against the brightness, and the way she looked at it was the way you looked at something that had just been given a new meaning you had not asked for and could not give back.

"My husband," she said. "When I told Vance, when I told him about Klaus, about the thermal event, about why I was willing to vote for a framework that I had reservations about, he said, " She stopped.

Mara waited.

"He said that Klaus's death was exactly the kind of loss the Accord was designed to prevent." Hartmann's voice was precise and very quiet. "He said that the people who built this framework understood grief. That they had done the arithmetic on grief. That the ratification window existed because we could not afford to let sentiment delay what necessity demanded."

She picked up the photograph. Held it in both hands, looking at the laughing man.

"He used it," she said. "He used Klaus to close me."

"Yes."

Hartmann set the photograph down with a care that was more controlled than gentleness. She crossed to the window, the same window where she had been standing when Mara came in, looking out at the lake, and stood there with her back to the room.

Outside, the water was the flat grey-silver of early morning, the far shore barely visible through a gauze of mist. A tram moved along the embankment, its yellow sides catching the weak light, its progress orderly and indifferent.

"If I delay my vote," Hartmann said, "Vance will know why within the hour."

"Yes."

"He'll move to isolate the delay. Procedural challenges. He has allies on the secretariat."

"I know."

"And the Accord itself, the framework, the binding commitments, the enforcement mechanisms, those are real. The climate provisions are real. Whatever Vance's reasons for building it, the structure exists and it works."

"It works for some people."

Hartmann turned from the window. Her face had settled into something Mara could not quite name, not resolution, not yet, but the thing that came before resolution, the moment when a person stopped arguing with what they knew and started deciding what to do about it.

"The session opens in twenty-two minutes," Hartmann said.

"I know."

"If you're wrong about the weighting tables, "

"I'm not wrong. But you have the data. You can verify it yourself. Yusuf Adeyemi's full dataset is on the drive. The methodology is documented. You can put it in front of any independent statistician in this building and have a preliminary assessment in forty minutes."

"Forty minutes after the session opens."

"Yes."

Hartmann looked at her for a long moment. Then she crossed to the desk, picked up her phone, and dialled a four-digit extension. When the line connected, she said, in the careful, uninflected German of formal address: "This is Ambassador Hartmann. I need a postponement of the German bloc's opening statement pending a technical review. Forty-five minutes. File it as a procedural hold under Article Twelve." A pause. "I'm aware of the timetable. File it." She ended the call.

The man in the grey suit opened the door without knocking. "Ambassador, "

"Article Twelve procedural hold. Forty-five minutes." Hartmann did not look at him. "Contact Director Vance's office and inform him that the German delegation requires a technical clarification before the opening vote. Use those words exactly."

The man's eyes moved to Mara. "And this individual, "

"Is with me." Hartmann picked up the drive from the laptop, held it out to Mara, and then seemed to reconsider. She set it back down. "Leave it. I need it for the review." She looked at the man in the doorway. "Ms. Voss has my authorisation. Now close the door."

He closed it.

Hartmann sat down at the desk, the first time she had sat since Mara arrived, and pulled the laptop toward her. Her hands on the keyboard were steady. That steadiness cost something; Mara could see it in the set of her jaw, the small muscle working there.

"Forty-five minutes," Hartmann said. "I need a name. Someone independent. Someone Vance cannot reach in forty-five minutes."

Mara had been thinking about this since Stuttgart. "There's a statistical modeller on the IPCC technical panel. Dr. Renata Ferreira, University of São Paulo. She's in Geneva for the session, I checked the delegate list last night. She has no affiliation with the Accord drafting team."

"You checked the delegate list."

"I've been planning this conversation for three days."

Hartmann looked at her with something that might, in a different moment, have been the beginning of respect. "Get Ferreira here. You have twenty minutes before Vance's people start making this room difficult to be in."

Mara was already moving toward the door. She had her phone out, Yusuf's number on the screen, Yusuf, who had Ferreira's direct line from the IPCC panel, who had been sitting in a café two streets away for the past hour waiting for exactly this call.

She stopped with her hand on the door.

"Ambassador." She turned back. "The Reykjavik Signal, what Vance knows, what he's been building toward. What do you want to do with that?"

Hartmann looked at the three printed pages on the desk. Then at the photograph of Klaus, laughing in the summer light, squinting at something off-camera that no one in this room would ever see.

"One thing at a time," she said. "First we establish whether the flaw is real. Then we decide what we owe the people it was designed to harm." She turned back to the screen. "Then we decide what we do about a man who has been governing in secret on behalf of something he cannot even name."

Mara went through the door.

In the corridor, her phone was already ringing, not Yusuf's number, not any number she recognised. The screen showed a Geneva prefix and seven digits she had never seen, and when she answered it, the voice on the other end was Elias Vance's, and he said her name in the tone of a man who had just been told exactly where she was.

The corridor smelled of recycled air and the faint chemical sweetness of fresh carpet, the Palais had been refurbished two years ago, and the smell had never quite left. Mara stood with the phone at her ear and said nothing.

"Don't hang up," Vance said.

She didn't. Not because she trusted him. Because she needed to know how much he knew.

"You've spoken to Hartmann." Not a question.

"Where are you?" she said.

"Forty metres behind you."

She turned. He was standing at the far end of the corridor, tall, slightly stooped at the shoulders in the way of men who had spent decades bending to hear people shorter than themselves. He wore no jacket. His shirt was the pale blue of a man who had dressed in a hurry or had stopped caring, and he was holding a small leather notebook against his thigh the way someone holds a thing they carry everywhere and no longer notice carrying.

He lowered his phone. She lowered hers.

He walked toward her. Not quickly. His footsteps on the carpet made almost no sound, which made the approach feel more deliberate than it was.

"I'm not here to threaten you," he said, when he was close enough that she could see the grey in his stubble, the dark beneath his eyes that spoke of months, not nights, of bad sleep.

"What are you here to do?"

"Talk." He glanced at Hartmann's door. "To both of you, if she'll allow it."

"She might not."

"She'll allow it." He said it without arrogance, just the flat exhaustion of a man who knew the people he worked with well enough to predict them. "She's been waiting for someone to explain it properly for two years. I should have explained it myself. That was a failure of judgment."

Mara looked at him. The word *failure* had not cost him anything, he had said it with the ease of a man who had already catalogued it alongside many others.

"Then explain it now," she said. "To me. Before we go in there."

He considered that for a moment. Then he nodded.

"The Signal." He said it the way you say a word you have said ten thousand times in private and almost never aloud. "You've seen the summary document."

"Enough of it."

"Then you know the intercept was real. The source was a deep-array hydrophone station off the Reykjavik coast, military grade, calibrated for submarine detection. What it received in November 2019 was not submarine traffic." He paused. "The signal lasted eleven minutes and forty seconds. It contained a recursive mathematical structure, self-referencing, base-twelve, with embedded prime sequences that could not have occurred naturally. Commander Lund's team ran seventeen independent verification passes. The probability of natural origin was, " He stopped himself. "It doesn't matter what the probability was. It was not natural. We have known this for twenty-two years."

The corridor was empty. Somewhere below them, in the great chambered rooms of the Palais, the session was preparing to open. Mara could feel it the way you feel weather, a pressure, a shift in the building's attention.

"And the Accord," she said. "The flaw in the weighting tables."

"Is deliberate." He said it without flinching. "Yes."

"You engineered scarcity for four billion people."

"I made a calculation." He held up the notebook. "Do you want to see it? Not a summary. The actual figures. I've been keeping them since 2020."

She didn't answer, which he took as yes. He opened the notebook, the pages were dense with handwriting, columns of numbers interspersed with dates, and occasional single words that she couldn't read quickly enough. The handwriting was small and even, the writing of a man who had been careful about this, who had wanted the record to be legible.

"The approaching intelligence, whatever it is, wherever it originated, is moving. The signal's directionality and the baseline Doppler shift give us a travel vector. Our best estimate, as of last year's recalculation, is twenty-six to thirty-one years before it reaches a position from which it can assess us directly." He turned two pages. "In that window, we need to present a species that is unified, resource-stable, and governable at scale. A species that has solved, or is credibly solving, its existential resource crisis." He looked up. "You understand what I'm saying."

"You're saying you decided which people to sacrifice to make the rest of us look civilised."

Something moved in his face. Not guilt, he had moved past guilt, she thought, into something quieter and more terrible.

"I'm saying the arithmetic did not offer a version where everyone survives the transition," he said. "I looked for one. I looked for eight years. The models don't produce it. A full equitable distribution of SOVEREIGN's resource governance, full parity across all regions, produces a stabilisation timeline that exceeds the contact window by eleven to nineteen years. We arrive too late. We are still a species in crisis when we are assessed." He turned another page. "A weighted distribution, the flaw, as you call it, produces stabilisation within the window. The Northern Hemisphere reaches demonstrable resource equilibrium. The system presents as functional."

"While the Global South dies."

"While the Global South is deprioritised." He heard himself. "While mortality in sub-Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia increases by a projected, " He turned to a specific page, the page he had clearly turned to many times, the crease worn soft. "Between forty and seventy million excess deaths over fifteen years. Excess above current trajectory."

She looked at the number. It was written in the same careful hand as everything else.

"And that," she said, "is the sacrifice you decided was acceptable."

"That is the sacrifice I decided was less terrible than the alternative." His voice was level. "If the approaching intelligence deems us ungovernable, if it looks at this species and sees a civilisation still tearing itself apart over water and arable land and energy, we have no precedent for what follows. None. We have thirty years of classified analysis and every model produces the same outcome range, and the lower bound of that range is extinction-class." He closed the notebook. "I chose forty to seventy million. Against a potential eight billion. That is the arithmetic."

"It's not arithmetic," Mara said. "It's a sentence. Passed on people who were never in the room."

"No one was in the room." His voice, for the first time, had something raw in it. "That's the nature of the decision. If I had put it to a vote, any vote, any body, it would have leaked, it would have caused panic, it would have destroyed the Accord before it could be built, and we would have nothing. No framework, no stabilisation, no chance." He looked at her steadily. "I am not asking you to approve of what I did. I am asking you to understand why a person might do it."

Hartmann's door opened.

She stood in the doorway, composed, as she always was, but her eyes went immediately to the notebook in Vance's hand, and Mara saw her register it.

"Elias," she said.

"Lena."

"Come in," Hartmann said. "Both of you.", -

The room felt smaller with three of them in it. The mist had thickened outside the window; the tram line on the embankment was empty now, the yellow cars gone somewhere further along their route. The photograph of Klaus stood on the desk, and Vance's eyes went to it and stayed there for a moment before he looked away.

He sat without being asked, in the chair across from Hartmann's desk, the chair Mara had not used. Mara stood near the window. She wanted the distance. She wanted to be able to see both of them.

"You've seen the data Mara brought," Vance said to Hartmann.

"I've seen enough to want an independent assessment."

"Ferreira," he said. "From the IPCC panel."

Hartmann didn't react to his knowing. "Yes."

"She'll confirm the flaw is real." He set the notebook on the desk between them. "I'm not here to dispute the data."

Hartmann looked at the notebook. She did not touch it.

"Then what are you here to dispute?" she said.

"Nothing." He spread his hands, large hands, reddened at the knuckles from cold water, from the long swims he took alone. "I'm here to explain. And to ask." He looked at Hartmann directly. "You signed the Accord because of Klaus."

Hartmann's jaw tightened. "Don't."

"I'm not using it against you. I'm saying I know why you signed, and it was the right reason. The climate provisions are real. The enforcement mechanisms are real. The framework will do what we said it would do, for the regions it prioritises." He paused. "I kept the Signal from you because I believed you would refuse to sign if you knew the full rationale. I was probably right. That was a decision I made, and I am not going to pretend it was anything other than a decision to deceive you."

The room was very quiet. Outside, somewhere below, a door closed with the heavy certainty of institutional architecture.

"The Signal," Hartmann said. "Tell me."

He told her. Not the version he had given Mara in the corridor, the compressed, careful version. The full version, or as full as it could be in the time they had. He told her about the hydrophone station, about Lund's seventeen verification passes, about the base-twelve recursive structure, about the Doppler shift and the travel vector and the twenty-six to thirty-one year window. He told her about the eight years of modelling and the stabilisation timelines and the number on the page he had turned to so many times that the crease had gone soft.

Hartmann listened without interrupting. Her face did not change in the way faces change when people hear something unbelievable. It changed in the way faces change when people hear something they have been half-expecting and have been hoping not to hear.

When he finished, she was quiet for a moment.

"You've known this since 2019," she said.

"Since 2020. It took six months to verify."

"Twenty-two years."

"Yes."

She looked at the notebook. This time she reached out and opened it, not to a specific page, just the first page she found, a column of figures dated March 2031. She looked at the numbers for a long moment. Then she closed it.

"The flaw," she said. "If I delay the vote, if Ferreira confirms the weighting tables, what happens to the Accord?"

Vance looked at his hands. "Depends on what you do with the confirmation."

"If I take it to the full session."

"The Accord collapses. The coalition fractures. We lose the enforcement mechanisms, the binding commitments, the climate provisions. All of it." He looked up. "And we lose the stabilisation timeline. We arrive at the contact window as a species still in crisis."

"Or," Mara said from the window, "we arrive at the contact window as a species that chose not to condemn four billion people to engineered scarcity to make ourselves look governable."

Vance looked at her. "You think that matters to whatever is coming?"

"I think it matters to us." She held his gaze. "And I think you used to think so too. Before you stopped sleeping."

He said nothing. That was, she thought, its own kind of answer.

Hartmann stood. She walked to the window and stood beside Mara, and for a moment both women looked out at the mist and the grey water and the empty embankment where the tram had been.

"The Accord as written is a lie," Hartmann said. "Not in its mechanisms. In its premise. It promises a governed world and delivers a culled one."

"It delivers a surviving one," Vance said.

"You don't know that." Hartmann turned to face him. "You have models. You have projections. You have a signal from something you cannot name, making an approach you cannot confirm, toward a judgment you cannot predict." Her voice was steady and very cold. "You have built a system of deliberate harm on a foundation of what you do not know, Elias. And you have done it without asking."

Vance stood. He picked up the notebook and held it against his chest, not a gesture of defiance, something closer to the opposite.

"I know," he said. "I know that. I have known it every day for fifteen years." He looked at her. "I am asking you now. That's why I'm in this room. Not to stop you. To ask you, before you act, to understand what it costs."

Hartmann looked at him for a long time. The muscle in her jaw worked once and was still.

"I understand what it costs," she said. "I understood the moment she showed me the table." She glanced at Mara. "The question is who bears the cost. And you decided that without us."

Vance's phone buzzed. He looked at it, a reflex, not a choice, and something shifted in his face. Not alarm. Something more complicated.

"Ferreira is in the building," he said. He looked at Hartmann. "She came in through the delegate entrance eight minutes ago. Someone called her." He looked at Mara. "Your epidemiologist."

Mara said nothing.

Vance put the phone in his pocket. He looked at the notebook in his hands, then set it on the desk, set it down with a deliberateness that felt, to Mara, like a man putting down something he had been carrying for a very long time and was not sure he could pick back up.

"The session opens in fourteen minutes," he said. "Whatever you decide, Lena, I won't move against you procedurally. I want that on record."

"There's no record here," Hartmann said.

"There's her." He looked at Mara. "That's enough."

He went to the door. He stopped with his hand on the frame, the same frame the man in the grey suit had stood in twenty minutes ago, in what felt like a different version of the morning.

"The Signal is real," he said. He was not looking at either of them. He was looking at the wall, or through it, at something neither of them could see. "Whatever you decide about the Accord, whatever you decide about me, that part is real. Something is coming. And we will have to answer for what we are."

He went out. The door closed behind him with the soft, expensive click of a room that had been designed to contain important conversations.

Hartmann stood very still. Then she picked up Vance's notebook from the desk and held it in both hands, not opening it, just holding it, feeling its weight, the years of it.

"Ferreira," she said. "How long does she need?"

"Twenty minutes for a preliminary read. She'll know within the first five whether the weighting is structural or incidental."

"And if it's structural."

"It's structural."

Hartmann set the notebook down. She looked at the photograph of Klaus, the summer light, the squint, the laugh caught at the wrong moment and preserved forever in a frame on a desk in Geneva while the world made its arrangements.

"He would have hated this," she said. "All of it. The secrecy. The arithmetic." A pause. "He would have said you can't save a species by deciding which parts of it don't count."

Mara said nothing. There was nothing to say that Hartmann hadn't already said better.

"Get Ferreira to this room," Hartmann said. "And find out what Vance meant by *won't move against you procedurally.*" She looked at Mara. "Because a man who says what he won't do is always thinking about what he still can."

The chamber filled from the back.

Mara watched it from the press gallery, a narrow horseshoe of tiered seating bolted to the upper wall of the Palais des Nations' main conference room, the kind of space that made you feel simultaneously important and irrelevant. Petra had gotten her in with a spare credential and a confident walk, the way Petra got into most places she wasn't supposed to be. The credential said *Agence France-Presse*. The photograph was close enough.

Below, the delegates were taking their seats in the slow, deliberate way of people who understood that being seen arriving was itself a form of statement. Nameplates caught the light, brushed aluminium, each country's name in both English and French, arranged in the horseshoe pattern that the UN's founders had chosen to suggest equality and that sixty years of practice had made into something more complicated. The room smelled of recycled air and the faint chemical sweetness of the simultaneous-translation headsets, hundreds of them racked in their cradles along the back of each desk.

Petra leaned close. "Ferreira make it?"

"She was in the anteroom when I left. She had four minutes with the weighting tables."

"Four minutes."

"She's fast."

Petra said nothing. She had her press tablet open on her knee, the screen dimmed to a grey whisper. She was not typing. She was watching.

The gallery was half-full, technical staff, a handful of NGO observers with lanyards in the pale green of civil society access, two journalists Mara recognized from the treaty beat. No one looked at anyone else. The room below held everyone's attention the way a fire does: not because it was beautiful, but because of what it might do next.

Mara found Vance.

He was standing at the far end of the chamber's floor level, against the wall behind the last row of delegate desks, in the space reserved for senior Secretariat staff. He had no notebook. He had his hands at his sides and his face arranged into the careful neutrality of a man who had spent thirty years learning to show nothing in rooms where everything was being watched. But he was very still, the particular stillness of someone who has stopped trying to manage an outcome and is simply waiting to see what the world does.

She had known him, she realized, for six years. She had attended twelve briefings he had run. She had written three compliance assessments that cited his framework documents. She had thought him thorough, precise, occasionally brilliant, and wholly committed to the institution. She had not been wrong about any of that. She had simply not known what the institution had been committed to.

The gavel came down, three times, the wooden sound flat and sharp in the high-ceilinged room.

"The Assembly is in session." The Secretary-General's deputy, a Singaporean diplomat named Tan whose voice carried without effort, settled into the chair at the head of the horseshoe. "This session is convened for the purpose of ratification of the Framework Accord on Coordinated Resource Governance, as amended. The floor is open for any procedural motions before the vote is called."

Silence.

The kind of silence that has weight.

Mara's hands were cold. She pressed them flat against her thighs.

Then Hartmann stood.

She stood the way she did everything, without announcement, without performance, with the simple physical fact of a woman who had decided to do something and was doing it. She was wearing the dark jacket she'd had on in the anteroom, the one that had dried from the rain into something that looked almost deliberate. Her delegate nameplate, *Germany / Allemagne*, caught the light as she reached for her microphone.

"Ambassador Hartmann. Germany." Deputy Tan's voice was careful. "The chair recognizes."

"Thank you." Hartmann's voice came through the room's speakers with a slight electronic warmth that made it sound, paradoxically, more human. "Before the vote is called, Germany invokes Article Nineteen of the General Assembly's procedural rules, the right to request formal technical review of any instrument presented for ratification where a member state has identified a material question of technical accuracy."

The silence lasted perhaps two seconds.

Then the room came apart.

Not loudly, this was the UN, not a parliament, but the sound of sixty delegates beginning to speak to their aides simultaneously produced a noise like a wave hitting shingle, a long rushing hiss of whispered consultation that rose and did not fall. Three delegates were on their feet. The Brazilian ambassador had his hand up. The Indian delegation's deputy chief leaned across to the chief and spoke directly into her ear, one hand cupped around his mouth.

Mara realized she was gripping the gallery railing.

"Order." Tan's gavel. "Order, please." The hiss subsided, not because it was finished but because the room understood that the next thing said from the chair would matter. "Ambassador Hartmann. Article Nineteen requires the invoking member to specify the nature of the technical question and to name a qualified reviewer. Is Germany prepared to do so?"

"Germany is." Hartmann had not sat down. She stood with both hands on the desk, her weight forward, the posture of someone who had no intention of being interrupted before she was finished. "The technical question concerns the resource-allocation weighting matrix embedded in the SOVEREIGN governance algorithm, specifically, whether the differential weighting applied to regional nodes in the Southern Hemisphere reflects a structural design decision or a calibration error. Germany has identified a qualified reviewer: Dr. Isabel Ferreira, computational systems architect, currently credentialed to this session as a technical observer."

"Ferreira," Petra said, very quietly. Not a question.

Mara nodded.

The Brazilian ambassador was recognized. He was a compact man with silver hair and a way of speaking that suggested he had been saving this particular sentence for some time. "Brazil wishes to understand the basis for Germany's concern. The SOVEREIGN framework has undergone eighteen months of technical review by the Accord's own committee. Are we to understand that Germany is questioning the adequacy of that process?"

"Germany is questioning one specific output of that process," Hartmann said. "Not the process itself. The distinction matters."

"With respect, "

"The distinction matters," Hartmann said again, and something in her tone closed the sentence like a door.

Tan let the silence sit for a moment. "The chair notes that Article Nineteen, once invoked, is not subject to a vote. It is a right of member states. The question before this session is the scope and duration of the technical review." He looked down at something on his desk, a procedural document, Mara assumed, the kind of thing that existed in a binder that no one read until the moment it became the only thing that mattered. "Article Nineteen, paragraph four, provides for a suspension of not less than forty-eight hours and not more than ninety-six. Germany is asked to specify."

"Seventy-two hours," Hartmann said.

Mara let out a breath she had not known she was holding.

Seventy-two hours. Not a rejection. Not a collapse. A pause, procedurally clean, legally unimpeachable, the kind of pause that could become a door or a wall depending on what happened inside it.

The chamber noise rose again, and this time it had a different texture, less shock, more calculation. Mara watched the delegates the way she watched a chess position after an unexpected move: not the piece that had moved, but everything else, the new pressure lines, the squares that had changed value.

The Nordic bloc was quiet and composed. The EU delegates were in rapid bilateral conversation. The US delegation, three people, two of whom Mara had never seen before, sat with the particular stillness of people receiving instructions through an earpiece. The African Union bloc, twelve delegates spread across the horseshoe, had turned inward, their chairs angled toward each other, and the Ghanaian ambassador, a woman Mara's mother's age, in a kente-cloth stole that was the only colour in the room that wasn't grey or navy, was speaking with a controlled urgency that Mara could see from the gallery but not hear.

She wanted to hear.

She looked at Vance.

He had not moved. He was still against the wall, hands at his sides. His face was still arranged into its careful nothing. But his eyes were on Hartmann, not with anger, not with calculation. With something that Mara, watching from above, could only call recognition. The look of a man watching a consequence arrive that he had known, on some level, was always coming.

He had told her he wouldn't move against Hartmann procedurally.

He had not said what he would do after.

"The chair accepts Germany's specification," Tan said. "Seventy-two hours, commencing at the close of this session. Dr. Ferreira is recognized as technical reviewer under Article Nineteen. The review will be conducted under the auspices of the Office of Treaty Compliance, "

Mara's breath caught.

", with findings to be presented to this body no later than", Tan checked the time on his desk panel, "eleven hundred hours, Friday. This session is suspended."

The gavel came down once, final, the sound of a clock starting.

The chamber erupted properly now, delegates on phones, aides crossing the floor at a near-run, the ambient noise rising to something that pressed against the gallery's low ceiling. Mara watched Vance push off from the wall and move toward the door with the unhurried pace of a man who had somewhere to be and did not intend to be seen rushing to get there. He did not look up at the gallery. He did not look back at Hartmann.

He went out.

"Office of Treaty Compliance," Petra said. She had stopped pretending not to type. "That's your office."

"Yes."

"Which means the review lands on your desk."

"Or my director's."

"Your director just walked out of the room." Petra looked at her. "Mara."

"I know."

"You understand what Tan just did."

"He didn't do it. It's procedural. It's automatic."

"It landed in your office automatically." Petra's voice was precise and not unkind. "You are going to be the analyst of record on a technical review of the system you just spent three days trying to prove is broken. With the woman who can confirm the break sitting in an anteroom two floors down." She paused. "That is either the best thing that has happened to you in this building, or it's a trap."

Mara looked at the floor of the chamber below, where Hartmann was fielding three conversations simultaneously, the Brazilian ambassador, two of her own aides, and a woman from the Secretariat legal office who had materialized with a tablet and an expression of controlled alarm.

Hartmann caught Mara's eye.

It was a fraction of a second, a glance upward that could have meant anything or nothing. But it was deliberate, Mara was certain of that. Hartmann had known exactly where she was sitting.

"It's not a trap," Mara said.

"How do you know?"

"Because if it were a trap, Vance would have stayed in the room."

Petra considered this. Then she closed her tablet and stood. "Seventy-two hours."

"Yes."

"Different kind than yesterday."

Mara thought about what Hartmann had said in the anteroom, before the session. *A man who says what he won't do is always thinking about what he still can.* She thought about the notebook Vance had set down on the desk and the way he had walked out of this chamber, not defeated, not finished, just repositioned. A man who had spent fifteen years building something did not stop building because a vote was suspended. He changed what he was building toward.

"I need to get to my office before he does," she said.

Petra was already moving toward the gallery stairs. "Then stop thinking and walk."

The chamber was still draining when Mara found the bench.

It was in the corridor outside the gallery, a wooden thing bolted to the wall between two fire-exit signs, the kind of bench that existed only to be sat on while waiting for something else. She sat on it now because her legs had made the decision before she did. The corridor was moving around her, aides with lanyards, a Secretariat security officer closing the gallery doors, a cluster of delegates from the Pacific bloc still in argument, their voices bouncing off the marble floor and arriving at her as noise without meaning.

She took out her phone.

Yusuf picked up on the second ring, which meant he was between patients. He always picked up on the second ring when he was between patients, first ring was too eager, third ring meant he'd had to find the phone, and Yusuf Adeyemi ran a clinic with the same precision he applied to everything except his own meals.

"Mara."

Just her name. The way he said it told her he'd been following the feeds.

"It's suspended," she said.

A pause. Not the Geneva kind, not the kind that meant calculation or repositioning. The kind that meant he was breathing.

"Suspended is not ratified," he said.

"No."

"So tell me what suspended means."

She leaned her head back against the wall. Above her, the ceiling was the particular institutional white of a building that had been repainted so many times the colour had stopped being a choice and become a condition. "Seventy-two hours. Technical review. The algorithm gets examined by an independent assessor, findings presented to the full body Friday morning."

"And the review lands where?"

"My office."

Another pause. Then, quietly: "Of course it does."

"Yusuf, "

"I'm not laughing. I'm thinking."

She could hear, behind his voice, the ambient texture of the clinic, a fan running, something metal set down on a hard surface, a child's voice somewhere further back that rose and then was answered by a woman's. She had never been to the clinic. She knew it from these sounds, from the way they changed depending on what time of day she called. Morning calls had traffic and birdsong through whatever window he left open. Afternoon calls had the fan. Evening calls had quiet, which meant he was the last one there.

"What do you see from your window?" she said.

"Right now?"

"Right now."

He took a moment. She knew he was actually looking, Yusuf was not the kind of man who answered a question like that without looking.

"The jacaranda is coming in," he said. "It's early this year. The whole street is going purple." A beat. "There's a queue at the water distribution point on the corner. Sixteen, seventeen people. They've been there since six this morning. The truck was supposed to come at eight." He paused. "It's half past two."

Mara said nothing.

"The woman at the front of the queue has a baby on her back," Yusuf said. "She's been standing in the same spot for six hours. She brought a plastic container, the kind you'd use for cooking oil. Twenty litres. She's going to fill it and carry it home on her head." He stopped. "That's what I see from my window."

The corridor around Mara had thinned. Two cleaners were moving along the far end with a cart, their voices low, working efficiently the way people work when they are invisible to the people around them.

"The Accord was supposed to fix that," Mara said. "That's what they said. Coordinated allocation, optimised distribution. No more queues."

"I know what they said."

"But the algorithm, "

"I know what the algorithm does." His voice was even. "Mara, I've been trying to get someone in that building to read my data for eight months. You read it in three days." A pause. "Don't tell me what the Accord was supposed to do. Tell me what you're going to do."

She looked at her hands. She had a small cut on the index finger of her right hand from the edge of a document wallet, the kind of cut you don't notice until you see it. She didn't remember getting it.

"I don't know," she said.

"That's honest."

"It's not enough."

"It's a start." She heard him shift, a chair, or the edge of a desk. "You've been in that office for ten years."

"Eleven."

"Eleven years. And you're good at it. You're very good at it. But I've watched you describe your job to people at conferences and I've never once heard you say you love it."

"Yusuf, "

"I'm not telling you to quit. I'm telling you that the thing you just did, three days, seventy-two hours, whatever it was, that wasn't compliance work. That was something else."

She thought about Hartmann in the anteroom. The photograph on the desk. *He died in the heat and I thought I was doing this for him.* She thought about Vance walking out of the chamber with his hands at his sides, unhurried, repositioning, a man who did not stop building. She thought about Kofi Asante's face when he'd handed her the document, the way he had looked at her as though he was passing something he could no longer carry.

"I'm not going back to the treaty office," she said.

She hadn't known she was going to say it until she had.

Yusuf didn't answer immediately. When he did, his voice was careful and not unkind. "What does that mean for Friday?"

"I'll do Friday. The review. I'll do it because it needs doing and because I'm the person who knows where the flaw is." She paused. "After Friday, I don't know."

"Okay."

"That's all you're going to say?"

"What do you want me to say?"

She almost smiled. "Something useful."

"Come to Nairobi," he said. "After Friday. Not to work. Just to come. See the jacaranda. Meet the woman with the cooking-oil container." A pause. "You've been solving problems in rooms with no windows. Come and see what the problems look like from outside."

Down the corridor, one of the cleaners had stopped to retie a shoelace, kneeling on the marble with the easy patience of someone who had learned not to hurry. The other waited without comment, cart handles resting in her palms.

"I'll think about it," Mara said.

"You'll think about it and then you'll call me at two in the morning to tell me you've decided to stay in Geneva."

"Probably."

"And then I'll tell you to come to Nairobi."

"Probably."

A beat of something that was not quite silence, the fan, the child's voice again, further away now, the ambient fact of a city continuing.

"Yusuf," she said. "The woman at the front of the queue."

"Yes."

"Is the truck coming?"

A pause. She could hear him looking.

"I don't know," he said. "It's not here yet."

She held the phone against her ear for another moment. Then she said goodbye and hung up.

The corridor was nearly empty now. The cleaners had moved on. The delegates were gone, dispersed into their bilateral conversations and their earpieces and their calculations. The gallery doors were closed. Through them, very faintly, she could hear the chamber being prepared for the next session, chairs straightening, microphone checks, the ordinary work of a room that did not know yet what it would be asked to hold.

She stood up.

The cut on her finger had stopped bleeding at some point without her noticing. She pressed it once with her thumb, feeling the clean edge of it, and then she put her phone in her pocket and walked toward the lift.

She had seventy-two hours. She knew what the flaw was and she knew where it was and she knew, with the particular cold clarity of someone who has spent eleven years learning how institutions protect themselves, exactly how hard the next three days were going to be.

What she did not know, and this was new, and strange, and not entirely unwelcome, was what came after.

The lift doors opened. She stepped in, pressed the button for the fifth floor, and watched the corridor disappear as the doors closed.

The review was waiting. Vance was somewhere in this building, already moving. And in Nairobi, a woman with a cooking-oil container was still standing at the front of a queue, waiting for a truck that had not come.

*Friday*, Mara thought. *First, Friday.*

The lift began to rise.

- **Regional identity (Swabia / Stuttgart)**  
  Stuttgart is the capital of Baden‑Württemberg and part of the **Swabian** cultural region, known locally for frugality, a distinct Swabian German dialect, and strong regional pride.[2]  
  Locals often refer to the broader region as **Schwabenland**, and Swabian dialect features softened consonants and altered vowels compared to standard High German.[2]  

- **Local cuisine & food vocabulary (Stuttgart / Swabia)**  
  Everyday and restaurant menus commonly feature **Maultaschen** (Swabian ravioli filled with minced meat, spinach, onions, and soaked bread) and **Spätzle**, soft egg noodles often served with meat dishes or in **Käsespätzle** (Spätzle baked or mixed with melted cheese and crispy onions).[2][1]  
  Traditional German staples like **Bratwurst**, **Sauerkraut**, **Sauerbraten**, and **Brezeln** (pretzels) are readily available in Stuttgart’s bakeries, markets, and beer gardens.[1][2]  

- **Climate and seasonal feel (Stuttgart area)**  
  Stuttgart experiences relatively **mild winters** where snow is possible but described as a “rare morning with snow,” making snowy days notable and photo‑worthy events for locals.[8]  
  The city has a comparatively high number of **sunny days, especially in spring and summer**, encouraging outdoor café culture, walks, and use of parks and vineyards on surrounding hillsides.[2]  

- **City geography & urban character (Stuttgart)**  
  Stuttgart lies in a **basin surrounded by hills**, which shapes its skyline with terraced housing, vineyards, and forested slopes visible from many streets and viewpoints.[3][2]  
  The city mixes **quiet residential districts** with a business‑focused center and highly visible car industry facilities; it is often characterized as having a “quiet strength” and understated, work‑oriented atmosphere rather than the nightlife intensity of Berlin.[3][10]  

- **Cultural life and institutions (Stuttgart)**  
  Stuttgart offers major **cultural institutions** including opera, ballet, and theater, forming a strong classical and high‑culture scene for residents.[10]  
  The city government supports youth cultural participation with initiatives like a **Culture Pass** giving 16‑year‑olds a €100 voucher to spend on art supplies or cultural events, tying everyday teen life to local museums, theaters, and concerts.[7]  

- **Big events and venues (Porsche Arena)**  
  Large concerts and shows are held at the **Porsche Arena**, a prominent indoor venue used for events such as “Symphony of the Earth” organized under the auspices of the Stuttgart Lord Mayor.[5]  
  Attendees typically experience arena‑style seating, amplified sound, and a mix of local and international acts; the arena is a recognizable landmark for sports and cultural performances.[5]  

- **Daily rhythm and social norms (German context relevant to Stuttgart)**  
  Everyday life heavily emphasizes **punctuality**; arriving 5–10 minutes early to appointments or social commitments is considered polite and respectful of others’ time.[1]  
  **Quiet Sundays** are a norm, with reduced noise and many shops closed, reinforcing a weekly rhythm where errands and shopping are concentrated on weekdays and Saturdays.[1]  

- **Conversation, politeness, and language use**  
  Common polite phrases include **“Guten Tag”** (good day), **“Bitte”** (please), **“Danke”** (thank you), and **“Entschuldigung”** (excuse me), used frequently in daily interactions from shops to public transport.[1]  
  People typically address strangers and authority figures with the formal **“Sie”**, switching to informal **“du”** only after explicit or implicit mutual agreement, reflecting a clear boundary between formal and informal social spheres.[1]  

- **Restaurant and payment customs**  
  In restaurants, servers **do not automatically bring the bill**; diners signal they are ready by asking **“Die Rechnung, bitte”** (the bill, please).[1]  
  Tipping around **5–10%** is customary, and the phrase **“Stimmt so”** is used when paying to indicate the server should keep the change, a small but characteristic bit of dialogue at the table.[1]  

- **Work–life texture (contemporary Stuttgart)**  
  A “realistic week” in Stuttgart often combines **office or technical work**, commuting via public transport, evening walks, and encounters with the city’s car culture (passing showrooms, test tracks, or employee parking lots full of German cars).[9]  
  Residents weave errands, supermarket runs, and café visits around structured work hours, with time‑efficient planning and an emphasis on using free time deliberately for leisure, exercise, or cultural events.[1][9]  

- **Visual and sensory city impressions**  
  Streets and plazas show a blend of **modern glass architecture and older stone or stucco buildings**, with tram lines, bus stops, and cycling lanes contributing to a sense of orderly movement through the city.[3][9]  
  On rare snowy mornings, the **crunch of snow underfoot**, muted traffic sounds, and visible breath in the cold air contrast with more typical mild, sunny days where outdoor seating, birdsong, and distant hum of traffic define the soundscape.[8][2]

sub_chapter_briefs.title: The Vote That Wasn't
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: Hartmann walks into the chamber and, before the ratification vote is called, invokes Article 19 of the UN Charter to request a formal technical review — a procedural suspension, not a rejection; the chamber erupts; Vance stands at the back, still, watching; Mara, watching from the press gallery where Petra has smuggled her, understands that the Accord is suspended but not dead, and that she has seventy-two hours of a different kind now.

sub_chapter_briefs.arc_beat: Act V — partial resolution: the immediate catastrophe is averted but the underlying crisis (the Signal, the flaw, the need for some answer) remains unresolved
sub_chapter_briefs.setting: The ratification chamber floor and press gallery, full assembly, delegates from forty nations
sub_chapter_briefs.emotional_tone: Stunned relief undercut immediately by the knowledge that this is a pause, not a victory — the emotional register of someone who has stopped a car from going over a cliff and is now standing on the edge
sub_chapter_briefs.connects_to_book_arc: The Accord is suspended rather than ratified or destroyed — honouring the novel's refusal of clean resolution; the Signal problem remains, meaning humanity still needs an answer, just not this one

sub_chapter_briefs.title: What Remains to Be Done
sub_chapter_briefs.beat: In the aftermath, Mara sits alone in the emptying chamber and calls Yusuf — not to report victory, but because she needs to hear his voice; she tells him the Accord is suspended and that she does not know what comes next; he tells her what he sees from his clinic window in Nairobi; she hangs up knowing she will not go back to the treaty office, and that she does not yet know what she will do instead.

sub_chapter_briefs.arc_beat: Act V — denouement: the protagonist's internal arc closes; she has not become Vance, has not destroyed herself, but is genuinely changed and genuinely uncertain
sub_chapter_briefs.setting: The emptying ratification chamber, Mara alone in a delegate's seat; Yusuf on the other end of a phone line in Nairobi
sub_chapter_briefs.emotional_tone: Quiet, exhausted, honest — not triumphant; the emotional register of someone who has done the right thing and discovered it does not feel the way they expected
sub_chapter_briefs.connects_to_book_arc: Closes Mara's arc (the private worry about institutional complicity is resolved — she chose differently when it mattered) while leaving the book's largest question open (the Signal, the approaching intelligence, what humanity will actually do) for the epilogues to carry
